title.en: Lutung Kasarung: The Langur Monkey Who Was a God
title.zh: 魯通·卡薩魯恩：原為神明的葉猴

region.en: Wangun and Pakuan Pajajaran, West Java (Sundanese country)
region.zh: 西爪哇旺恩與帕庫安·巴查查蘭（巽他之地）

texts.period: Sundanese chronicle tradition (Raffles 1817, vol. II ch. X, quoting the Sunda annals)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X (the Lutung Kasarung narrative of the Sunda traditions)

summary.en: Kuwu Mangkubumi sends a pellet-shooter to fell what he takes for a large black monkey on the pandi tree — and the 'monkey' speaks: 'Don't shoot at me; go home and tell your master to come here himself.' Prabu Lutung Kasarung comes down, is offered to two elder daughters who refuse him, and is accepted gladly by the youngest, Niai Purba Sari — at whose wedding he lays aside the black monkey's skin and resumes his former beautiful appearance, establishing the line of Pakuan Pajajaran.
summary.zh: 庫烏·芒庫布米遣獵手射擊潘迪樹上的『大黑猴』——『猴』竟開口：『莫射我；回家告你主人親自前來。』普拉布·魯通·卡薩魯恩下樹相見；兩位長女皆拒嫁之，唯幼女妮艾·普爾巴·沙莉欣然接納——婚禮之上，他褪去黑猴之皮，恢復本來俊美容貌，帕庫安·巴查查蘭王朝由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Sundanese founding legend (Carita Parahyangan tradition as recorded by Raffles); animal-husband motif with divine identity.

texts.canonical_translation: Raffles, History of Java (1817), English; paraphrase

narrative.en:
The Sunda traditions that Raffles recorded in 1817 preserve West Java's founding myth in a form the lowland Javanese chronicles never tell: the god who comes as a monkey.

BEGINNING: THE SPEAKING MONKEY. Kuwu Mangkubumi establishes his youngest daughter, Purba Sari, in the interior near the gadug tree, and sets a pellet-shooter to work the district. One day the shooter sees on the great pandi tree what looks like a large black monkey, and takes aim; the creature speaks: 'Don't shoot at me; you had better go home and tell your master to come here to me himself.' The shooter returns aghast, and his master comes to the tree, where Prabu Lutung Kasarung descends and talks with him — a being of such extraordinary accomplishment that the Kuwu takes him home delighted.

MIDDLE: THE CHOICE OF DAUGHTERS. Wishing to attach so wondrous a creature to his house, the Kuwu offers him first to the eldest daughter, who refuses; then to a younger, who refuses likewise. Only the youngest of all, Niai Purba Sari, accepts him with great pleasure — the marriage goes to the daughter humble enough to take the suitor as he appears.

END: THE SKIN LAID ASIDE. When Niai Purba Sari becomes his wife, he lays aside the black monkey's skin and resumes his former, beautiful appearance; he receives the name of Niang Galarang, establishes himself at Pakuan Pajajaran — where the inscribed stone stands — and governs there. His wife becomes pregnant; he leaves the government to his ministers and withdraws to Bukit Padang as a Pattala; and their son, Silawangi, will grow into the great king of the Sundanese chronicles.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) grounds Pakuan Pajajaran, the Sundanese royal capital, in a divine-visitor marriage; (2) makes the acceptance of the humble appearance the test of rightful bride (the youngest-daughter motif); (3) ties kingship to the withdrawal of the god-founder into ascetic retreat; and (4) supplies the Sundanese counterpart to Java's Janggala-Kediri genealogies. The episode's social geometry repays attention: the Kuwu's household tests the suitor's appearance twice and both elder daughters decline, so that the divine visitor is accepted only by the youngest — the standard folktale marker of the daughter undervalued by her family, whose acceptance is rewarded with the god's true form and, through her son Silawangi, with the kingship of Pajajaran itself. The narrative also fixes two toponyms of the Sundanese landscape, the kampung Wangun and the kampung Tagur founded by the couple, and ends with the founder's characteristic withdrawal: as soon as the succession is secure, Niang Galarang leaves the seat of government to his ministers and removes to Bukit Padang as a Pattala, the ascetic retreat that later Sundanese tradition reads as the model of royal completion. In the full pantun tellings the monkey shape is the punishment of a heavenly exile, and the marriage that restores his form is the last condition of his return — the West Javanese version of the exiled-god theme that the Arjunawiwaha states in courtly verse.
narrative.zh: 拉弗爾斯1817年所錄巽他編年傳說保存了西爪哇開基神話：神以猴身而來。庫烏·芒庫布米置幼女普爾巴·沙莉於內地加都古樹旁；獵手見潘迪樹上『黑猴』而瞄準，猴竟人言。魯通·卡薩魯恩下樹，才華驚人，庫烏攜歸。庫烏欲以女妻之：長女拒、次女拒，唯幼女妮艾·普爾巴·沙莉欣然接受。婚後神褪猴皮復其真容，得名尼揚·加拉朗，建都帕庫安·巴查查蘭（即今碑石之地）；妻有孕後，他將國政委於大臣，退隱布基特·巴當為隱者；其子西拉萬吉將成巽他編年史之偉王。功能：以神婚立帕庫安王都、以『接納平凡外表』為擇婿考驗（幼女母題）、以神主退隱繫王權於苦修、並成爪哇章格拉-諫義里譜系之巽他對應。

functions: Grounds Pakuan Pajajaran, capital of the Sundanese kingdom, in a divine-visitor marriage
Youngest-daughter test: the rightful bride accepts the suitor as a monkey
The god-founder's withdrawal into ascetic retreat as the pattern of Sundanese kingship
Sundanese counterpart to the Javanese dynastic genealogies

variants.name: Later Sundanese pantun epic (Lutung Kasarung)
variants.summary: The expanded telling makes Lutung Kasarung the exiled son of Guru Batara Sunan Ambu, sent to earth and monkey-shaped until his mission of restoring justice is done.

variants.name: Bible-animal-husband parallels
variants.summary: Beast-suitor whose monstrous skin hides divinity; compare the Javanese Keong Emas snail-bride in reverse.

secondary_sources.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java
secondary_sources.citation: Raffles 1817, London: Black, Parbury and Allen — vol. II ch. X, the Sunda tradition block.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Raffles, History of Java, vol. II (1817)

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Founding legend of the Sundanese royal tradition; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: The pellet-shooter came to the large pandi tree, and observing on it what he supposed to be a large black monkey, wished to shoot it; whereupon Prabu Lutung Kasarong, whom he mistook for the monkey, thus addressed him: 'Don't shoot at me; you had better go home and tell your master to come here to me himself.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Kuwu took him home highly delighted; in course of time he wished to present him to his eldest daughter, and on her refusing to accept of him he offered him to a younger one, but neither would receive Prabu Lutung Kasarong. He then gave him to the youngest of all, named Niai Purba Sari, who accepted of him with great pleasure.

When Niai Purba Sari became his wife, he laid aside the black monkey's skin with which he was clothed, and immediately resumed his former and usual beautiful appearance. He afterwards received the name of Niang Galarang, and established himself at Pakuan Pajajaran, where the Balutulis (inscribed stone) now is, and which was the seat of government of the Maha Raja.

title.en: Prabu Silawangi and the Hall of Eight Hundred Pillars
title.zh: 西拉萬吉王與八百柱大殿

region.zh: 西爪哇帕庫安·巴查查蘭

texts.period: Sundanese chronicle tradition (Raffles 1817, vol. II ch. X)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X (Silawangi narrative)

summary.en: Silawangi, the beautiful son born to Niai Purba Sari, removes to Sumedang Larang, marries many wives, and returns to Pakuan Pajajaran by way of the south coast, embarking at Nusa Kambangan. Established as Raja amid great rejoicings, all the princes from the river Chi Pamali to Java Head submit to him; he builds the pentebanj audience-hall 'Sangaka Domas' of eight hundred pillars, and the interior hall 'Rarasmi Kanchana' of golden flowers — and the tradition gives him one hundred and fifty wives and one hundred and fifty sons-in-law made great officers.
summary.zh: 妮艾·普爾巴·沙莉所生之美貌王子西拉萬吉，先移居蘇梅當·拉朗，廣娶眾妻；後經南海岸、自努薩·坎班甘登舟還都帕庫安·巴查查蘭。即位慶典連宵，西自芝帕馬利河至爪哇角諸王皆服；乃建八百柱大殿『桑嘎卡·多馬斯』、內殿『金花殿』——傳說並言其有一百五十妻、一百五十婿皆為高官。

sensitivity.note: Sundanese royal charter legend; the 800-pillar hall is Pajajaran's remembered splendour.

passages.text: When the time was come, Niai Purba Sari brought forth a son of the most exquisitely beautiful features, to whom she gave the name Silawang'i. When Silawangi grew up, he removed from Pakuan Pajajaran to Sumedang Larang, where he was soon afterwards married, first to one raja's daughter and then to the daughter of the Peng'gawa of that place, so that he had many wives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: On his arrival at Pakuan Pajajaran, Prabu Silawangi established himself as Raja; all the princes from the river Chi Pamali beyond Java Head submitted to him. He then built without the kraton a hall of audience, called Sangaka Domas, or the hall of eight hundred pillars; and in the interior of the kraton another, called Rarasmi Kanchana, or that of golden flowers.

The tradition goes on to relate that Prabu Silawangi had one hundred and fifty wives, and that his sons-in-law, of whom there were also one hundred and fifty, were made great public officers — the Sundanese memory of Pajajaran's widest power.

title.en: Sangkuriang and Dayang Sumbi: The Boat That Became a Mountain
title.zh: 桑古里揚與達揚·松比：化為山巒的小舟

region.en: Tangkuban Perahu, near Bandung, West Java
region.zh: 西爪哇萬隆附近覆舟山（唐庫邦·珀拉胡）

texts.period: Sundanese oral legend; recorded in 19th-20th century collections

source.work: The legend of Sangkuriang and Dayang Sumbi (Sundanese oral tradition, Tangkuban Perahu etiology)

summary.en: The princess Dayang Sumbi, exiled for breaking a vow, is courted by the dog Tumang who is really a god; her son Sangkuriang, sent hunting, kills the dog without knowing it is his father, and serves its liver to his mother, who strikes his head and drives him into the world. Years later the marked wanderer returns and woos his own mother; she recognizes the wound, sets him the impossible task of damming the Citarum and building a great boat in one night, and cheats the finishing dawn — and the kicked, half-finished boat lies overturned on the plain as the mountain Tangkuban Perahu.
summary.zh: 因違誓而遭放逐的公主達揚·松比，被化身為犬的神明托芒求愛；其子桑古里揚奉命出獵，不知那犬正是生父而殺之，以其肝烹於母親——母親擊其首，將其逐入世界。多年後，帶傷的流浪者歸來向親母求婚；母親認出傷痕，令其一夜之間築壩截芝塔龍江並造巨舟，又設計騙過完工的黎明——被踢翻的半成之舟倒扣於平原之上，是為覆舟山。

sensitivity.note: Oedipal-type West Javanese foundation legend; treated as literature, cited carefully.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the Sundanese oral legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
Sangkuriang is West Java's great etiological legend — the mountain Tangkuban Perahu ('the overturned boat') above Bandung is the story's fossil.

BEGINNING: THE VOW AND THE DOG-HUSBAND. The beautiful Dayang Sumbi has vowed to marry whoever returns her discarded shuttle; the dog Tumang fetches it, and she must keep the vow — in the fuller tellings Tumang is a god in dog-form. She bears a son, Sangkuriang, and the dog remains as the household's hunter.

MIDDLE: THE LIVER DISH. Sent hunting, the boy returns empty-handed; on his mother's chiding, he shoots the dog Tumang, not knowing it is his father, and cooks its liver for her meal. When the truth is told, Dayang Sumbi strikes him on the head with the rice-ladle, leaving the mark by which he will one day be known, and the boy wanders off into the world.

END: THE BOAT AND THE FALSE DAWN. Years later a powerful young stranger courts the still-beautiful Dayang Sumbi; she recognizes the scar and understands that this is her son. To delay the incest she sets a task fitted to his giant's strength: in a single night he must dam the Citarum river and finish a great boat to carry the lake away. Supernatural helpers raise the dam and shape the boat; fearing his success as dawn comes, she spreads a red cloth (in some tellings lights the eastern sky) so that the cocks crow early — the spirits flee, the work stops short, and Sangkuriang, cheated, kicks the boat over. It lies overturned on the plain as the mountain; the dammed valley remains as the Bandung basin, and the mother retreats to the hill-top to wait for the day the boat rises again.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) etiologizes Tangkuban Perahu and the Bandung plain; (2) polices the incest boundary through the riddle of the unrecognizable son (the wound-mark motif); (3) dramatizes the false-dawn trick as female resistance; and (4) grounds Sundanese identity in a landscape-story told at every school and tourist site in West Java. The landscape completes the argument. Tangkuban Perahu's distinctive profile — a tilted ridge that does look like an overturned hull — is the story's standing exhibit, and the Bandung basin below is the lake the dam would have made; local tellings add that Dayang Sumbi waits on the summit for the day the boat is righted and the flood returns. The false-dawn device links the legend across the island to the Roro Jonggrang cycle, in which the same trick of pounded rice and kindled fires defeats a supernatural suitor's deadline; in both, the woman's wit beats the ogre's or the giant's labour, and the punishment lands on the deceiver in a form that fixes her in the landscape. The Sangkuriang telling is the darker of the two because the suitor is also the son: the wound-mark that lets the mother recognize him is the same mark her ladle made, so that the legend binds its incest horror to the memory of a punishment already given — the mother has struck the boy once, and the blow returns wearing courtship's clothes.
narrative.zh: 桑古里揚乃西爪哇第一大釋源傳說——萬隆上方之覆舟山即其化石。開篇：達揚·松比誓嫁拾回梭子者；神化犬形之托芒拾之，遂成婚生子桑古里揚。中段：少年出獵空手而歸，受母嗔責，射殺家犬托芒——不知即其父——以其肝烹食；真相既明，母以飯杓擊其首（留下他日相認之疤），逐之於世。結尾：多年後偉岸青年向仍美豔之母求婚；母認疤而知為己子，遂設巨力方能完成之難題：一夜之內築壩截芝塔龍江、造巨舟以載湖而走。妖眾助其築壩造舟；黎明將成之際，母展紅布（或燃東天）令雞早鳴——妖眾驚散、工程中止，桑古里揚受欺而踢翻其舟；舟覆於平原是為覆舟山，築壩之谷留為萬隆盆地，母親退居山頂，等待小舟再起之日。功能：釋覆舟山與萬隆平原之由來、以『不可辨之子』維護亂倫禁忌、以假晨之詐寫女性抵抗、並以山水故事奠定西爪哇認同。

False-dawn trick as female resistance within the suitor's test

passages.text: Dayang Sumbi, exiled for breaking her vow, is courted by the dog Tumang, who is a god in dog-form; her son Sangkuriang grows up in the household of his unknowing father. Sent hunting, the boy shoots the dog and serves its liver to his mother; when the truth is told she strikes him on the head with the rice-ladle — the mark by which he will later be known — and he wanders off into the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend of Sangkuriang; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend; not verbatim.

passages.text: Years later the marked wanderer courts his own mother; she sets the giant's task of damming the Citarum and finishing a great boat in one night, then cheats the finishing dawn with a spread cloth so that the cocks crow early. The spirits flee, the boat lies half-finished, and Sangkuriang's kick turns it over on the plain — the mountain Tangkuban Perahu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend; not verbatim.

title.en: Situ Bagendit: The Lake That Swallowed the Miser's Village
title.zh: 巴根迪湖：吞沒吝嗇婦之村

region.zh: 西爪哇加魯特巴根迪湖

source.work: The legend of Situ Bagendit (Sundanese oral tradition)

summary.en: The rich widow of the village refuses every beggar; one day an old woman asks only for water and is mocked, and warns that the village's wealth will not save it. That night the springs burst: the rice-fields, the barns, the widow seated on her treasure, and the whole village sink under a new lake — Situ Bagendit, the 'lake of the widow,' where fishers say the drowned rice-bins still lie.
summary.zh: 村中富婦拒絕一切乞者；一日老嫗只討一瓢水而遭譏，乃警告：財富救不了此村。當夜泉眼迸裂：稻田、糧倉、坐在財寶上的寡婦乃至全村，盡沉於新湖之下——是為巴根迪湖（『寡婦之湖』），漁人言湖底猶有沉沒的糧倉。

sensitivity.note: Sinking-village flood legend; hospitality-test type in the Sundanese highlands.

passages.text: The widow of the village turns away every beggar; to the old woman who asks only for water she answers with mockery, and receives a warning that her wealth will not save the place. That night the springs burst open: the rice-fields, the granaries, the widow on her treasure and the whole village sink beneath a new lake — Situ Bagendit, the widow's lake — where the drowned barns, fishers say, are still to be found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend of Situ Bagendit; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend; not verbatim.

title.en: Prabu Siliwangi: The Vanished King of Pajajaran
title.zh: 普拉布·西利萬吉：消失的巴查查蘭之王

region.en: Pakuan Pajajaran and the West Javanese mountains
region.zh: 帕庫安·巴查查蘭與西爪哇群山

texts.period: Sundanese dynastic legend (Pajajaran line); medieval and early modern tradition

source.work: The legend of Prabu Siliwangi (Sundanese dynastic tradition, Pakuan Pajajaran line)

summary.en: In Sundanese memory the last great king of Pakuan Pajajaran, Prabu Siliwangi, becomes more legend than history: the archetype of the just ruler of the Parahyangan, credited in tradition with retreating from the fallen capital into the mountains rather than submit, and henceforth present in the highlands as a hidden presence — the name invoked by every later West Javanese court and shrine that claimed his authority.
summary.zh: 在巽他人記憶中，帕庫安·巴查查蘭末代偉王普拉布·西利萬吉漸成傳說：巴查查蘭（Parahyangan，『眾神之地』）公正之王的原型；相傳都城傾覆之際，他不肯臣服而隱入群山，此後便以隱形之力存於高地——日後西爪哇每一宮廷與聖所凡欲承其權威者，皆呼其名。

sensitivity.note: Dynastic memory-legend; kept at the level of attested tradition, avoiding invented specifics.

passages.text: In Sundanese tradition the last great king of Pakuan Pajajaran, Prabu Siliwangi, is remembered as the archetype of the just ruler of the Parahyangan — the 'land of the gods' — his name the standard by which later West Javanese courts claimed authority.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sundanese dynastic tradition as preserved in the chronicle material recorded by Raffles (1817) and later collections; not verbatim.

passages.text: Tradition credits him with refusing submission when the kingdom fell, withdrawing from the capital into the mountains, and remaining thereafter a hidden presence in the highlands — the vanished king who legitimizes every shrine and court that invokes his name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sundanese dynastic tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: The Shuttle and the Vow: Dayang Sumbi's First Promise
title.zh: 梭子與誓言：達揚·松比的初諾

texts.period: Sundanese oral legend (prelude of the Sangkuriang cycle)

source.work: The shuttle-vow prelude of the Sangkuriang cycle (Sundanese oral tradition)

summary.en: Weaving at her loom, the princess Dayang Sumbi drops her shuttle through the floor-hole and vows that whoever brings it back — man, animal, or god in any shape — shall be her husband. A dog brings it up the stair; the vow is kept, the dog-god Tumang becomes her husband, and the union that scandalizes her father sends her into exile — where she will bear the boy whose own vow, years later, will shake the mountains.
summary.zh: 公主達揚·松比織機之上梭子墜落，遂發誓：無論何人（人或獸、或神之任何形體）拾還此梭，即嫁之為夫。拾梭而來者是一隻狗；誓言必守，犬神托芒遂為其夫；此樁醜事觸怒其父，她被逐出家門——在那裏她將誕下那個多年後以誓言撼動群山的男孩。

sensitivity.note: Vow-kept-literally motif; prelude of the Sangkuriang cycle.

passages.text: Weaving at her loom, Dayang Sumbi drops the shuttle and vows that whoever returns it — man, animal, or god in any shape — shall be her husband; a dog brings it up the stair, and the vow is kept to the letter. The dog-god Tumang becomes her husband, the union scandalizes her father's house, and she is exiled — bearing in time the son Sangkuriang, whose own promise, years later, will shake the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend (shuttle-vow prelude); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend; not verbatim.
